questions.q: What principle drives the access table in this lesson?
options: Least privilege — a role gets exactly the access its job requires, no wider
Every employee gets full access to every element by default
Access is assigned alphabetically by role name
Only executives are ever granted any data access
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly names least privilege as the design principle, scoping Sales and Support to their own accounts/tickets rather than the whole table.

questions.q: Who can access Payments.CardToken, and under what condition?
options: Only Risk & Compliance, with every access logged and audited
Every employee, with no logging required
Only Sales Reps, for their own accounts
No one — not even Risk & Compliance can access it
questions.explain: The access table restricts CardToken, the Restricted-tier element, to Risk & Compliance only, with audited access.

questions.q: Why does Payments.CardToken have the shortest retention period (13 months) of any element in the program?
options: Sensitivity and retention move together — the most Restricted element has the least justification to be kept past its specific purpose (the chargeback window)
13 months is simply the minimum SQL Server allows for any column
CardToken is actually the least sensitive element in the program
Retention periods are assigned at random
questions.explain: The lesson states explicitly that the most sensitive data gets the shortest justified retention window, tying CardToken's short period to its Restricted classification.

questions.q: What principle does the retention schedule follow, per this lesson?
options: Data minimization — keeping data only as long as it serves a specific, named purpose
Maximizing storage to keep all data forever
Deleting all data immediately after it's created
Retention periods based solely on file size
questions.explain: The lesson ties the retention schedule directly to the data minimization principle already taught in this career path's Security & Privacy Governance course.

questions.q: Why does this lesson treat access and retention as one combined policy rather than two separate documents?
options: Because the same classification (e.g. CardToken's Restricted tier) drives both who can see an element and how long it's kept
Because access and retention have nothing to do with each other
Because only retention policies are required; access policies are optional
Because combining them was purely a formatting choice with no underlying logic
questions.explain: The lesson's closing section explains that the same sensitivity driving the access table also drives the retention table for the same element, making them one policy conceptually.
